THE WATERED GARDEN, Maud Stepney Rawson.—Full of incident as it undoubtedly is, "The Watered Garden" interests us chiefly in its clever character studies. That of Mrs. Pardew, the fussy little woman with the big ambitions, kind where it suited her convenience, hard as nails when there was anything to be gained, is particularly well drawn. In the first chapter she engages Bettina Gale, ostensibly to be her "lady gardener" at an old country place just purchased by the Pardews; but Bettina soon finds she is expected to do a dozen things as well. However, she finds time to remake and care for the lovely gardens, and it is here, in the descriptions of this old-world garden, that Mrs. Stepney Rawson charms us most. One feels in every line her knowledge and love of the country. There is plenty of romance as well, for Bettina has several admiers. But Mrs. Rawson tells us in a preface that a woman's life does not end
IDLENESS

There is no dearer lover of lost hours
Than I.
I can be idler than the idlest flowers;
More idly lie
Than noonday lilies languidly afloat,
And water-pillowed in a windless moat.
And I can be
Stiller than some grey stone
That hath no motion known.
It seems to me
That my still idleness doth make my own
All magic gifts of joy's simplicity.

regularly visits the mess of the Hanover Uhlans, a smart lancer regiment raised entirely in the province and never stationed out of it. It used to be said that the regiment point-blank refused to serve in other Prussian territory, and the fact remains that it never does. Another Hanoverian regiment was granted an honour by the Emperor thirteen years ago that never fails to attract comment from English visitors. On the sleeves of their uniform they wear the word "Gibaltar," commemorating the part the regiment played in the famous siege of that fortress while serving with the British in 1782.
